Photograph: Akhtar Soomro/Reuters Harry Brook Sri Lanka stun England with second-highest ODI chase despite Brook’s 202
 Liyanage hits six for win with one ball to spare
 England captain’s record innings not enough
 Taha Hashim Thu 22 Oct 2026 12.37 EDT Last modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 15.42 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Harry Brook pulverised his way to the fastest double hundred in ODI history and still ended up on the losing side. This was an absurd contest, with Sri Lanka hauling down a target of 430 in Rawalpindi, the second-highest successful chase in the history of the format. Only that magical 438 game, 20 years ago, trumps it.
 Pavan Rathnayake, Dasun Shanaka and Avishka Fernando were the headliners, turning it around for Sri Lanka after they were reduced to 24 for two. Rathnayake top-scored with 130, Fernando struck 97, and Shanaka, with 97 of his own, was the most brutal of the lot. After being taken apart with the ball, his revenge act included eight sixes.
 England v Sri Lanka: Brook makes history in men’s tri-series cricket ODI – live Read more None of the trio were there at the close as England suddenly found themselves back in it, eight needed by Sri Lanka off the final over. Josh Tongue rattled the stumps of Dunith Wellalage and Eshan Malinga with consecutive deliveries, but Janith Liyanage walloped a six down the ground to close the night, finishing his stay on 61 with a ball to spare.
 So a sublime piece of work, even by Brook’s high standards, came in vain. His footwork was the standout during his 202, tap-dancing across the crease as he ramped, scooped and sliced the ball behind both sides of the wicket with remarkable ­consistency. It took him 114 balls to reach 200, beating Shubman Gill’s 117-ball effort for India against West Indies three weeks ago.
 “It was a nice innings; unfortunately it doesn’t mean anything now,” he said. “Being on the losing side, it has no value whatsoever in my eyes.”
 England’s captain will also have to reflect on the makeup of his side for the next two games of this tri-series after back-to-back defeats. A ­notable selection call could so easily have been forgotten in victory. Adil Rashid, expensive against Pakistan on Tuesday , was left out for Liam Dawson as England opted for the skiddier left-arm option.
 Tom Banton punched his way to 50 for the fourth game in a row, but the first major act was the third-wicket stand between Joe Root and Brook. The pair hopped into the DeLorean and went back to January in Colombo, when they put on 191 in a series decider against Sri Lanka. Brook began slowly, just 13 off his first 24 deliveries, but took advantage of the part-timers, thumping Kamindu Mendis and Liyanage to reach his half-century off 42 balls.
 Quick Guide A record-breaking ODI: in numbers
 Show Harry Brook’s 202 was England’s highest ever one-day international score, beating Ben Stokes’ 182 against New Zealand in 2023.
 • It was the highest ever score and first double century by a batter in an ODI defeat, the previous record being Charles Coventry’s 194 not out for Zimbabwe against Bangladesh in 2009.
 • 429 for four was England’s fourth-highest ODI total, the record being 498 for four against the Netherlands in 2022. It was their highest outside England against a Test-playing nation.
 • The 859 runs scored in total was the second highest ODI aggregate and the highest in a game involving England, beating the 807 in a February 2019 win over the West Indies.
 • Brook’s 144 runs in boundaries – 21 fours and 10 sixes – surpassed Jos Buttler’s England record of 124 in that game. The two teams combined for 93 fours and 552 runs in boundaries in Rawalpindi, both records for a one-day international match.
 • Sam Curran broke his own England record for the most runs conceded in an ODI innings. Curran's two for 103 from nine overs exceeded the 98 runs he gave up in a 2023 loss to the Windies.
 • There were an ODI record-equalling four century partnerships – Brook with both Joe Root and Will Jacks for England, and Sri Lanka’s Pavan Rathnayake with both Avishka Fernando and Dasun Shanaka. It was the fifth ODI with four such stands, the most recent coming in July as England beat India at Lord’s. PA 
 Highest successful run chases in men's ODIs 
 Sri Lanka's astonishing effort on Thursday slots in as the second-highest successful chase in men's one-day international history …

 Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback. Milestones follow Root every time he bats nowadays and this time it was the mark of 8,000 ODI runs. He quietly accumulated as Brook began to torment Sri Lanka’s frontliners as well. While Root miscued on 69, Brook reached his hundred from 75 balls.
 As Will Jacks joined in and bashed a few himself, it became clear that an enormous total was on, as was the double for Brook. He moved from a ton to 150 in 22 balls; he took 17 more to reach 200. A cute ramp off Liyanage was a fitting stroke to get there. The only thing missing was a red-inker, with Brook perishing off the final ball of the innings.
 View image in fullscreen Harry Brook guides the ball to the off side during his record-breaking 202 off 116 balls. Photograph: Sameer Ali/Getty Images Lost within Brook’s genius was Jacks’s power, his unbeaten 66 ­taking 30 balls. Wellalage was the only bowler to escape Brook’s wrath, not conceding a boundary off the 27-year-old. Two for 56 has never looked so good.
 Sri Lanka lost two wickets quickly. Tongue bowled Kamindu with a corker and Kusal was gone before facing, run out by Gus Atkinson’s fingertips at the non-striker’s end. But Rathnayake and Avishka refused to collapse.
 Quick Guide Who else scored a double century and ended up on the losing side?
 Show Harry Brook is far from the first player to score more than 200 runs in an international innings and end up on the losing side – it happened to West Indies legend Brian Lara on three occasions. Azhar Ali and Len Hutton shared the feeling of scoring a double ton and ending up losing a Test by an innings. 
 The Englishman is, however, the first to endure the feeling in a one-day international.

 Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback. This was still a flat pitch to enjoy and Sri Lanka, hours earlier, had ­chosen to chase. The third-wicket pair put on 166, with Rathnayake particularly brutal when the ball went short. Avishka fell just shy of a hundred, returning a catch to Jamie Overton, but Shanaka kept up the rhythm. All while England’s great leg-spinner sat on the bench.
 At 250 for three, with 16 overs left, Sri Lanka were far better placed than England had been at the same stage, but it still felt so very far away. Rathnayake reached his century off 87 balls, thriving with that low-hands setup at the crease, and England failed to find a quiet over or two.
 Shanaka blitzed Sam Curran’s moon ball as he passed 50 and with 109 needed off 60 Sri Lanka finally looked the more likely victors. A tiring Rathnayake could not beat long-on against Curran and Shanaka fell on the boundary against Dawson. But Liyanage remained, keeping England winless in the series. Just staggering.
